newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH NBP BLASTS GOVERNMENT FOR BANKING LAW DELAY.
newsitem.headline: POLISH NBP BLASTS GOVERNMENT FOR BANKING LAW DELAY.

text.p: The National Bank of Poland's (NBP) president on Tuesday accused the government of delaying work on a draft banking law which was submitted by the central bank in 1994 to ensure the system's safety.

NBP President Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz said the ruling coalition was more concerned about passing a new central bank charter and deciding what people would sit on policy-making boards than overhauling the outdated banking sector regulation.
"Probably...this parliament will not look at the banking law before the elections," she told a news conference.

"This means there is more interest in working on the NBP's charter and looking at how many and which members of parliament would sit on the monetary policy board, the banking commission or other banking supervision authorities than in working for the safety of the banking system in Poland," she said.
Gronkiewicz-Waltz said the bank could not submit the banking bill to parliament directly and the government had failed to do so for three years.

She said that any government formed after the parliamentary polls due in September would probably have more pressing issues to deal with and would delay work on the bill until mid-1998 at the earliest.

She said that cooperation between the central bank and the U.S. government's USAID, along with other organisations, had yielded a solid base for a modern banking supervision system, which has been written into the banking law draft.
The draft's regulations envisage an independent body for banking supervision and guarding against unfair competition between banks.
It would also regulate more closely the origins of bank capital and the ownership structures of banks, preventing the dangerous expansion of so-called internal loans.
"Supervision authorities...must be able constantly to determine bank ownership structures," Gronkiewicz-Waltz said.
She said implementation of the banking law would make banks safer for Poles and help accumulate savings deposits, which would in future be used to finance Poland's economic growth.
